title: Seven sorrows
hook: the prophecy, the flight, the loss, the road, the cross, the pietà, the tomb
carry: a sword shall pierce thy soul

segments.voice: Yesterday, Theotokos, Mother of God, and torches in the streets of Ephesus. Your line was a claim about her son.

Mary and Joseph carry their baby into the temple in Jerusalem, as the Law asked of new parents when the days of purification were over. A happy, ordinary visit. An old man named Simeon, who has been promised he won't die before he sees the Lord's Christ, takes the baby in his arms and blesses God. Then he turns to Mary and says something no new mother wants to hear. In the Douay-Rheims: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce, that, out of many hearts, thoughts may be revealed." The family walks home with that sentence. Catholics have spent centuries asking what the sword turned out to be.
screen: `A NEWBORN IN THE TEMPLE.` → `AN OLD MAN, SIMEON.` → `A SWORD SHALL PIERCE.`

segments.voice: Tradition counts seven. The first is that prophecy. The second, the flight into Egypt: fleeing at night with a newborn, refugees, because a king wants him dead. The third, losing him. Jesus is twelve, and on the way home from Jerusalem they realize he's not in the group. Three days of searching. When they find him in the temple, Mary says: "Son, why hast thou done so to us? behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." That's a parent's voice after three days of fear. The fourth, meeting him on the road to the cross; the Gospels don't describe that moment, it comes from tradition and the Stations of the Cross. The fifth, standing at the cross. The sixth, holding his body when it's taken down. The Gospels don't describe that either; artists call it the pietà, from the Italian for pity, or devotion. The seventh, the tomb: laying him in the rock and walking away. The Gospels tell the burial but don't name Mary there. So four of the seven are scenes where the Gospels put Mary, and three come through tradition and prayer. A religious order founded in Florence, the Servants of Mary, spread the devotion, and the Church keeps the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows on September fifteenth, the day after the feast of the Cross. What the devotion holds on to: Mary's faith wasn't a shield against grief. She wasn't spared. She was pierced, seven times, and stayed.
screen: `THE PROPHECY, THE FLIGHT, THE LOSS.` · `THE ROAD, THE CROSS.` · `THE PIETÀ, THE TOMB.` · `FAITH ISN'T A SHIELD AGAINST GRIEF.` · then, large: `THY OWN SOUL A SWORD SHALL PIERCE.`

segments.voice: Let one sorrow of your own come to mind, big or small, old or new, and hold it the way you'd hold something fragile in both hands, without trying to solve it or talk yourself out of it. Mary didn't make her sorrows go away; she kept them, and kept going. If you pray, you can hand this one to her, and ask her to hold it with you.
Seven sorrows. The prophecy, the flight, the loss, the road, the cross, the pietà, the tomb: Mary's grief, counted and kept. Today's word.
Your line: a sword shall pierce thy soul. Simeon said it on a happy day, to a new mother. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Our Lady of Sorrows on 15 September, and some pray the chaplet of the seven sorrows, meditating on each one with a short set of prayers.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 2:35 and 2:48 given from memory; confirm.

The carry 'a sword shall pierce thy soul' is the index wording, not the Douay-Rheims word order ('thy own soul a sword shall pierce'). The script quotes the DR in the hook and teach and keeps the carry exact. Keeper may want the index line adjusted.

Five from the Gospels: prophecy (Luke), flight (Matthew), loss (Luke), cross (John), burial (the Gospels, with Mary's presence inferred from 'the women'); the descent from the cross into her arms and the meeting on the road are traditional. The script says 'five of the seven come from the Gospels'. Confirm the count is fair, since Mary's presence at the burial is not explicit.
Michelangelo's Pietà: completed c. 1499, when he was about 24; the only work he signed (on the sash). Confirm. Softened in review to 'the only work he is known to have signed'.
Servite Order founded c. 1233 in Florence by seven founders. Our Lady of Sorrows, 15 September (the day after the Exaltation of the Holy Cross). Confirm.
